sub_answers.sub_question: How does mirror symmetry breaking from Coulomb displacement and charge-dependent nuclear forces affect ANC-to-width mapping?
sub_answers.text: The Coulomb interaction breaks isospin symmetry and affects mirror mass differences relevant to ANC-to-width comparisons [d83088s0p0].

sub_answers.sub_question: What errors arise from assuming peripheral dominance and single-particle structure when using ANCs to predict widths?
How does model dependence in ANC extraction (optical potentials, reaction mechanism) contribute to uncertainty?
sub_answers.text:
Uncertainties arise from the choice of isospin-nonconserving Hamiltonian and effective charge-dependent nuclear forces used in models that extract ANCs [d16198s0p0].
Short-range correlations and their treatment in those models contribute to uncertainties in extracted quantities [d16198s0p0].
Microscopic residual interactions and the specifics of charge-dependent NN potentials used in structure calculations affect level structures and related observables that feed into ANC determinations [d148071s0p0].

sub_answers.sub_question: Why can ANC-based methods fail for broad resonances or overlapping resonances where single-level approximations break down?
What are the limitations of neglecting channel coupling and continuum contributions when using ANC-derived widths?
How are ANC-derived resonance widths used in calculating thermonuclear reaction rates for stellar nucleosynthesis?
sub_answers.text: ANC-derived information is combined with indirect methods to determine absolute astrophysical factors and thus accurate thermonuclear reaction rates for stellar nucleosynthesis [d36408s0p0].

sub_answers.sub_question: In what ways do ANC constraints aid the analysis of astrophysical proton-capture reactions near the drip line?
How do ANC-based predictions influence the interpretation of experimental data for exotic, short-lived nuclei?
sub_answers.text: ANC-based determinations of absolute cross sections help resolve inconsistencies among direct and indirect measurements for reactions that affect neutron production in stars [d36408s0p0].

sub_answers.sub_question: What advantages do ANC methods offer compared with direct width measurements for narrow resonances?
sub_answers.text: ANC methods provide an indirect approach to obtain absolute reaction rates when direct measurements at astrophysical energies are inconsistent or experimentally inaccessible [d36408s0p0].

sub_answers.sub_question: How have ANC-based predictions been validated against measured resonance widths in well-studied mirror pairs?
What is the formal definition of an asymptotic normalization coefficient (ANC) in nuclear physics?
sub_answers.text: An asymptotic normalization coefficient (ANC) is a quantity used to determine the absolute value of nuclear reaction cross sections by characterizing the amplitude of the tail of a bound-state wave function relevant for peripheral reactions [d36408s0p0].

sub_answers.sub_question: What is a mirror nucleus and what are the typical symmetry relations between mirror pairs?
sub_answers.text: A mirror nucleus is one member of a pair of nuclei related by exchanging protons and neutrons, and mirror pairs exhibit correlations in ground-state properties such as separation energies and charge radii [d110027s0p0].

sub_answers.sub_question: How is a resonance width defined in terms of decay probability and scattering theory?
What is the theoretical link between ANCs of bound states and widths of mirror resonances?
sub_answers.text: ANCs of bound states are used together with indirect methods such as the Trojan Horse Method to determine astrophysical reaction rates and thus connect bound-state amplitudes to resonance behavior in related reactions [d36408s0p0].

sub_answers.sub_question: Which experimental observables are commonly reported as ANCs in nuclear data compilations?
sub_answers.text: ANCs are commonly reported as values extracted from transfer reaction measurements, such as alpha-transfer reactions [d69413s0p0].

sub_answers.sub_question: What is the single-particle relation between ANC, spectroscopic factor, and single-particle wave function amplitude?
How does the R-matrix formalism express resonance widths in terms of reduced width amplitudes or channel radii?
What role do Coulomb-modified asymptotic forms play in converting proton ANCs to mirror neutron resonance properties?
How are ANCs extracted experimentally via peripheral transfer reactions such as (d,p) or (3He,d)?
sub_answers.text: Deuteron stripping to resonance states can be formulated using a surface integral representation that enhances the peripheral part of the amplitude relevant for extracting asymptotic information from transfer reactions [d24171s0p0].

sub_answers.sub_question: What approximations are involved in using single-channel potential models to compute ANCs and widths?
sub_answers.text: The surface-integral formalism demonstrates that a conventional CDCC volume matrix element can be written in terms of a peripheral surface matrix element and an auxiliary matrix element that determines the contribution of the nuclear interior [d24171s0p0].

sub_answers.sub_question: In what ways do isospin-symmetry breaking effects such as Coulomb displacement energies and charge-dependent components of the nuclear force modify the quantitative relation between measured asymptotic normalization coefficients (ANCs) and proton or neutron resonance widths? Give specific mechanisms and scaling laws.
sub_answers.text:
Coulomb interactions shift mirror-state energies and thus alter the relation between measured ANCs and proton resonance widths via Coulomb displacement energies that change barrier penetration factors and scaling with charge; this manifests as direct Coulomb effects dominating some energy shifts [d83088s0p0].
Charge-dependent nuclear forces and isospin-symmetry breaking terms modify ANC–width mapping by introducing additional effective interaction terms that affect overlap amplitudes and can alter extracted widths at the level relevant for mass-splitting systematics [d16198s0p0].
Corrections to simple Coulomb treatments are generally small for some observables but non-negligible for others, and non-Coulomb ISB terms can change extracted parameters by amounts comparable to the uncertainties in symmetry-energy-related quantities [d83088s0p0].

sub_answers.sub_question: What systematic biases and numerical errors occur when one extrapolates a measured ANC to predict scattering or decay widths under the assumptions of strict peripheral reaction dominance and a single-particle (independent-particle) overlap function? Identify contributions from interior amplitude, spectroscopic factors, and non-single-particle correlations.
sub_answers.text:
Neglecting interior overlap amplitude leads to bias because short-range correlations and interior structure modify spectroscopic strength away from a pure single-particle overlap [d16198s0p0].
Use of a single-particle overlap ignores charge-dependent effective forces and pairing contributions that redistribute strength and produce spectroscopic-factor differences that alter width predictions [d16198s0p0].
Peripheral-dominance assumptions can miss contributions from non-peripheral emission and pre-equilibrium dynamics that change fragment composition and thus affect extracted amplitudes in reaction observables [d147854s0p0].

sub_answers.sub_question: How sensitive are ANC extractions to model choices in reaction analyses (e.g., optical-model parameter sets, DWBA vs. CRC vs. CDCC, transfer kinematics), and how do these sensitivities propagate into uncertainties in the width predicted from the ANC? Provide typical magnitudes and sources of model-dependent variance.
sub_answers.text:
ANC extractions are sensitive to model inputs such as reaction mechanism treatments and kinematics, because differences in transport and reaction modeling change predicted yields and asymmetries used to infer structure information [d147973s0p0].
Optical-model or dynamical treatment choices map into observable variations through altered predicted particle and fragment flows and emission spectra, affecting extracted amplitudes and therefore widths [d40012s0p0].
Model-dependent variance arises from sensitivity to momentum-distribution assumptions and high-momentum tails, which change predicted particle yields and thus propagate into ANC-based width uncertainties [d45165s0p0].

sub_answers.sub_question: Under what conditions do ANC-based width predictions break down for resonances that are broad or sit in energy regions with nearby states (overlapping resonances)? Explain failures of the single-level Breit–Wigner or R-matrix single-pole approximation and specify observable signatures (line-shape distortion, energy-dependent phase shifts).
sub_answers.text:
ANC-based single-pole approximations break down when resonances are broad or closely spaced because level interference and channel coupling invalidate the single-level Breit–Wigner or single-pole R-matrix assumption, leading to line-shape distortions [d52115s0p0].
Overlapping states produce observable deviations such as distorted line shapes and modified energy-dependent shifts driven by direct Coulomb effects and differences in channel strengths, which affect extracted phase behavior and resonance parameters [d52115s0p0].

sub_answers.sub_question: What errors are introduced by ignoring coupling to other reaction channels and the non-resonant continuum when converting ANCs into resonance widths? Detail contributions from channel-channel coupling, doorway states, non-resonant background, and continuum discretization to misestimation of widths.
sub_answers.text:
Ignoring coupling to other channels and the non-resonant continuum biases width estimates because channel–channel coupling and doorway-state mixing redistribute decay strength away from the single-resonance amplitude [d52115s0p0].
Non-resonant background and dynamical effects from retarded fields or anisotropic interactions alter particle yields and spectral shapes, thereby changing inferred widths when continuum contributions are neglected [d40012s0p0].
Discretization or inadequate representation of the continuum and neglected short-range correlations modify strength distributions and can systematically misestimate widths derived from ANC information [d16198s0p0].

sub_answers.sub_question: Describe how asymptotic normalization coefficients (ANCs) are converted into resonance partial widths and then incorporated into thermonuclear reaction rate formulas (e.g., narrow-resonance and Hauser–Feshbach approximations) for stellar nucleosynthesis calculations.

Explain how ANC constraints reduce uncertainties in R-matrix or reaction-model fits for proton-capture reactions on proton-rich isotopes (near the proton drip line), and give examples of specific reactions or isotopes where ANC data critically alter the S-factor extrapolation.

Describe how ANC-derived width estimates are used to interpret cross section or decay-spectra measurements for short-lived, proton- or neutron-rich nuclei produced in fragmentation or transfer experiments, including how they guide resonance assignment and spin-parity determination.

List the practical benefits of using ANC-determined partial widths instead of attempting direct lifetime or width measurements for very narrow resonances (e.g., improved extrapolation to astrophysical energies, reduced beam-time, lower systematic error sources), and quantify typical precision gains where available.

Summarize case studies comparing ANC-predicted resonance widths to experimentally measured widths in mirror-nucleus pairs (or mirror decays), detailing which mirror pairs were used, methods of mirror-symmetry application, and how closely ANC-based predictions matched measured values.

Provide a precise, textbook-style definition of the asymptotic normalization coefficient (ANC) used in nuclear physics: state how it appears in the large-radius behavior of the radial overlap or bound-state wave function, its normalization convention, and the typical equation relating ANC to the single-particle Whittaker (or Coulomb) function and spectroscopic factor.
sub_answers.text: The asymptotic normalization coefficient (ANC) is the amplitude that multiplies the large-radius tail of a bound-state radial overlap or single-particle wave function and determines its normalization at asymptotic distances [d148282s0p0]. The ANC enters observables for peripheral reactions because the long-range radial integral that controls capture or transfer at low energies is largely determined by this asymptotic amplitude [d148282s0p0]. The ANC is conventionally defined by matching the overlap or bound-state radial wave function to the Whittaker (or Coulomb) bound-state solution at large radius so that the physical radial function equals the ANC times the Whittaker (or Coulomb) function in the asymptotic region [d148282s0p0]. The ANC is related to the single-particle Whittaker tail and the spectroscopic factor through a product in which the squared ANC equals the spectroscopic factor times the squared single-particle asymptotic amplitude obtained from the Whittaker solution (spectroscopic-factor × single-particle ANC^2) [d148162s0p0].

sub_answers.sub_question: Define a mirror nucleus in nuclear-structure terms (same mass number A, proton and neutron numbers interchanged) and list the expected symmetry relations between mirror pairs, including isospin symmetry, Coulomb energy shifts, level ordering similarities, and typical deviations (e.g., energy shifts, spectroscopic factor differences).
sub_answers.text: A mirror nucleus pair consists of two nuclei with the same mass number A and with proton and neutron numbers interchanged between the members of the pair [d83088s0p0]. Mirror pairs are expected to exhibit approximate isospin symmetry in their nuclear structure, leading to similar level ordering between partners apart from electromagnetic effects [d83088s0p0]. Coulomb interactions produce energy shifts (Coulomb energy shifts) between mirror levels that break the exact symmetry and can modify level spacings and ordering [d83088s0p0]. Typical deviations from perfect mirror symmetry include level energy shifts and differences in spectroscopic strengths due to Coulomb and other isospin-symmetry-breaking interactions [d83088s0p0].

sub_answers.sub_question: Give a clear operational definition of a resonance width both as a decay probability (Γ related to lifetime τ by Γ=ħ/τ and partial widths for specific channels) and in scattering theory terms (width as the imaginary part of an S-matrix pole, Breit–Wigner parameterization, and in R-matrix language as reduced width times penetrability).
sub_answers.text: The resonance width Γ is the decay probability expressed as an energy; it is related to the lifetime τ of the resonant state by Γ = ħ/τ and can be decomposed into partial widths for specific decay channels [d35654s0p0]. In scattering theory a resonance width appears as the imaginary part of the energy position of an S-matrix pole in the complex energy plane, with the pole position giving the resonance energy and width [d35654s0p0]. The Breit–Wigner parameterization represents a resonance by a peak whose width parameter corresponds to Γ and describes the energy dependence of cross sections near the resonance [d35654s0p0]. In R‑matrix language a resonance width is expressed as the product of a reduced width and a channel penetrability factor, connecting the internal structure to the external decay probability [d35654s0p0].

sub_answers.sub_question: Describe the theoretical connections proposed between ANCs for bound states and the widths of corresponding mirror resonances: cite the mechanism (analytic continuation of overlap functions, charge-symmetry of nuclear forces), the typical proportionality or formulae relating squared ANC to proton partial width (including Coulomb/penetrability factors), and conditions/limitations of this mirror-ANC–width relation.
sub_answers.text: Theoretical connections between ANCs for bound states and widths of mirror resonances are built on analytic continuation of overlap functions and on charge symmetry of the nuclear force linking mirror bound and unbound mirror states [d148282s0p0][d148162s0p0]. The typical relation equates the squared proton partial width of a mirror resonance to the squared ANC of the mirror bound-state overlap multiplied by appropriate Coulomb penetration or penetrability factors that account for the barrier and phase-space [d148282s0p0][d35654s0p0]. Proportionality formulae therefore relate the squared ANC to the proton partial width after including Coulomb/penetrability corrections and channel geometry factors [d148282s0p0][d35654s0p0]. The mirror-ANC–width relation holds under conditions of dominant peripheral overlap and approximate charge symmetry, and it is limited when nonperipheral contributions, strong isospin-symmetry breaking, or large model-dependent interior contributions are important [d148282s0p0][d148162s0p0].

sub_answers.sub_question: List the experimental quantities and data products that are reported or used to extract ANCs in nuclear data compilations: peripheral transfer and knockout cross sections, extracted ANCs from DWBA or CRC fits, reported spectroscopic factors, reduced widths, astrophysical S-factors, and the typical compiled numerical forms and units given in databases or papers.
sub_answers.text: Experimental quantities and data products reported or used to extract ANCs include peripheral transfer and knockout reaction cross sections analyzed at low momentum transfer [d36408s0p0]. Extracted ANCs are obtained from DWBA or coupled-reaction-channel (CRC) fits to these cross sections and are often reported alongside spectroscopic factors and reduced widths inferred from the same analyses [d36408s0p0][d148162s0p0]. ANCs are also used to determine astrophysical S-factors for radiative capture reactions, and combined analyses (e.g., ANC plus Trojan Horse Method) are reported to produce absolute astrophysical rates [d148282s0p0][d36408s0p0]. Numerical compilations typically present extracted ANC values, spectroscopic factors, reduced widths, and S-factor values with units appropriate to the quantity (ANCs as fm^{-1/2} or equivalent, spectroscopic factors dimensionless, widths in energy units such as eV) in papers and databases [d36408s0p0][d148282s0p0].

sub_answers.sub_question: Derive the quantitative relation in a single-particle model between the asymptotic normalization coefficient (ANC), the spectroscopic factor (S), and the amplitude (normalization) of the single-particle radial wave function — including the dependence on orbital angular momentum and channel radius used to define the single-particle bound-state wave function.

Provide the R‑matrix expression for a resonance partial width in terms of the reduced width amplitude (gamma or γλc), channel radius a, and penetration factor (or shift function) — show how the observed width Γ relates to γ² and the energy dependence near a resonance pole.

Explain how Coulomb-distorted asymptotic wave functions modify the analytic connection between proton ANCs and the properties of mirror neutron resonances — specifically how Coulomb functions (Whittaker/W and irregular F,G) and Coulomb barrier penetrability alter ANC-to-width conversions.

List and evaluate the experimental procedures and observables used to extract ANCs from peripheral transfer reactions (e.g., (d,p), (3He,d), (7Li,t)), including choice of beam energy to ensure peripheral kinematics, DWBA/ADWA analysis, optical model inputs, and how absolute normalization yields the ANC.

Enumerate the key assumptions and limitations when using single-channel local potential models to compute ANCs and resonance widths — e.g., neglect of coupling channels, choice of geometry and depth for Woods–Saxon potentials, absence of core excitation, spectroscopic factors treated as constants, and sensitivity to channel radius and matching radius.

In what ways do Coulomb-induced shifts and charge-symmetry-breaking nuclear interactions modify the theoretical relation between asymptotic normalization coefficients (ANCs) and resonance partial widths, and what quantitative corrections have been proposed for mirror nuclei comparisons?
sub_answers.text: The Coulomb interaction breaks isospin symmetry and produces shifts that modify mirror comparisons relevant for asymptotic properties of nuclear states [d83088s0p0].

sub_answers.sub_question: Which systematic and model errors occur when extracting resonance widths from ANCs under the assumptions of strictly peripheral reactions and pure single-particle overlap (e.g., using spectroscopic factors), and how large are these biases for typical light‑ion capture or transfer reactions?
sub_answers.text: Electromagnetic dissociation theory shows that higher‑order electromagnetic effects and nuclear interactions can bias extraction of structure observables when assumptions of peripheral single‑particle dominance fail [d147877s0p0].

sub_answers.sub_question: How do choices in reaction model input—such as specific optical-model potentials, bound-state form factors, and assumed reaction mechanisms (DWBA vs CDCC vs R-matrix)—propagate into uncertainties in ANC values, and what sensitivity studies quantify these contributions?
sub_answers.text: Reaction‑model inputs such as optical potentials and bound‑state form factors affect observable cross sections and extracted structural quantities through their treatment of distortions and final‑state interactions [d3996s0p0].

sub_answers.sub_question: What physical mechanisms cause ANC-based width estimates to break down for wide resonances or closely spaced (overlapping) levels (for example, energy-dependent level shifts, strong channel mixing), and how does multi-level R‑matrix or full continuum coupling alter the ANC→width mapping?
sub_answers.text: Strong medium modifications of resonance self‑energies, such as the Delta self‑energy, can strongly reduce cross sections and thus alter the mapping between asymptotic strength and widths for broad or in‑medium resonances [d3996s0p0].

sub_answers.sub_question: To what extent does ignoring explicit coupling to other open channels and nonresonant continuum (background poles, continuum–continuum coupling) bias partial-widths inferred from ANCs, and which observables or calculations can diagnose and correct for these missing continuum and channel-coupling effects?
sub_answers.text: Neglecting explicit coupling to other open channels and the nonresonant continuum can bias inferred partial widths because background contributions and continuum–continuum couplings affect observed strengths and shapes in reaction observables [d147877s0p0 d3996s0p0].

sub_answers.sub_question: What procedures convert resonance partial widths obtained from asymptotic normalization coefficients (ANCs) into thermonuclear reaction rates (e.g., resonant reaction rates, resonance strengths ωγ and contributions to astrophysical S-factors) used in stellar nucleosynthesis models?
sub_answers.text: Resonance partial widths are converted into resonance strengths ωγ and resonant reaction rates used in stellar models by using the measured or inferred partial widths to compute resonance strengths that dominate the reaction rate at astrophysical temperatures [d11376s0p0].

sub_answers.sub_question: How are ANC constraints applied to the analysis of proton-capture reactions on weakly bound or unbound isotopes (for example, proton captures on 22Al, 27P, or 69Br) near the proton drip line to reduce uncertainties in resonance energies and proton partial widths?
sub_answers.text: ANC constraints are used to reduce uncertainties in proton-capture resonance properties by providing external information on overlap amplitudes that inform proton partial widths and thus narrow the uncertainty in resonance strengths entering reaction-rate calculations for proton-rich nuclei relevant to explosive nucleosynthesis [d31520s0p0][d120397s0p0].

sub_answers.sub_question: When experimental data for very short-lived nuclei are sparse, how do ANC-based theoretical predictions—derived from transfer reaction measurements or mirror-structure extrapolations—change the interpretation of measured cross sections, resonance strengths, or decay branching ratios for exotic systems?
sub_answers.text: When experimental data for very short-lived nuclei are sparse, indirect constraints (such as those replacing adopted indirect resonance strengths) can change the interpreted contribution of a given resonance to astrophysical rates and motivate direct measurements to resolve discrepancies [d114332s0p0][d11376s0p0].

sub_answers.sub_question: For narrow resonances that are difficult to measure directly, what practical benefits do ANC-based methods (using peripheral transfer reactions, single-particle reduced widths, or R-matrix fits constrained by ANCs) provide in determining proton partial widths, level spectroscopic factors, and resulting reaction-rate contributions?
sub_answers.text: For narrow resonances that are difficult to measure directly, ANC-based methods provide practical benefits by constraining proton partial widths and hence resonance strengths, which improves estimates of reaction-rate contributions in temperature regions of astrophysical interest [d114332s0p0][d11376s0p0].

sub_answers.sub_question: Which studies comparing ANC-derived proton widths with directly measured resonance widths in established mirror pairs (for example 13N/13C, 17F/17O, or 23Al/23Ne) demonstrate agreement or systematic discrepancies, and what specific metrics (width ratios, spectroscopic factors, or resonance energy shifts) were used in those validations?

Provide a precise mathematical definition of the asymptotic normalization coefficient (ANC) used in nuclear reaction theory, including how it appears in the asymptotic form of a bound-state radial wavefunction and any conventional normalization factors (Whittaker/Coulomb functions) used.
sub_answers.text: The asymptotic normalization coefficient (ANC) is the amplitude that multiplies the asymptotic tail of a bound-state radial overlap wave function for a nucleon + core configuration in a nucleus [d148282s0p0]. [d17772s0p0].

sub_answers.sub_question: Define a mirror nucleus in nuclear-structure terms, list examples (e.g., 17O/17F, 7Li/7Be), and describe the expected isospin and Coulomb-symmetry relations that connect energy levels and spectroscopic factors of mirror partners.
sub_answers.text: A mirror nucleus pair is an isospin mirror where proton and neutron numbers are interchanged while total mass number is the same, as exemplified by the 7Li/7Be mirror pair discussed in capture-reaction studies [d28818s0p0].

sub_answers.sub_question: Give the formal definition of a resonance width Γ in quantum scattering and decay: relate Γ to the decay probability per unit time, to the lifetime τ, and to S-matrix pole properties or Breit–Wigner parameterizations used in scattering theory.

Explain the theoretical relationships and approximations that connect the ANC of a bound-state in one nucleus to the proton (or neutron) decay width of its mirror unbound state, citing mechanisms such as mirror symmetry, Coulomb barrier effects, single-particle spectroscopic factors, and analytic continuation of overlap functions.
sub_answers.text: Mirror symmetry is used to relate capture reactions in mirror systems, for example using the isospin mirror process 7Li(n,γ)8Li to inform 7Be(p,γ)8B calculations [d28818s0p0]. [d148282s0p0]. The ANC of a weakly bound final state largely determines low-energy radiative-capture S-factors, so ANCs extracted for a bound mirror state can be used to constrain reaction amplitudes for the corresponding unbound mirror resonance under mirror-symmetry assumptions [d148282s0p0]. Coulomb dynamics and the charged-particle barrier strongly affect peripheral transfer amplitudes and therefore must be treated correctly when relating mirror ANCs to proton widths or capture observables [d57152s0p0].

sub_answers.sub_question: List the specific experimental quantities that nuclear data tables or compilations report as ANCs (e.g., absolute ANC values C, squared ANC C^2, channel radii, extracted spectroscopic factors, reaction cross sections or asymptotic normalization extracted from transfer or breakup experiments) and note the typical units and uncertainties reported.
sub_answers.text: Published analyses report absolute ANC values extracted from theory or experiment and use these ANCs to fix reaction-model couplings in EFT or to determine astrophysical factors [d28818s0p0]. [d36408s0p0]. Transfer and breakup experiments are used to extract ANCs for specific states, and such extractions can yield differing ANC values with sizable error bars depending on analysis conditions [d69413s0p0]. [d36408s0p0].

sub_answers.sub_question: Derive the quantitative relationship linking an asymptotic normalization coefficient (ANC) to a spectroscopic factor and the normalization of the single-particle radial wave function for a bound state in a mean-field potential; include how node structure and single-particle reduced width enter the expression.
sub_answers.text: The asymptotic normalization coefficient (ANC) is the amplitude that fixes the long-range normalization of the bound-state proton wave function and thereby largely determines external capture observables near threshold [d148282s0p0]. The reduced matrix element for radiative capture involves the single-particle bound and scattering radial wave functions obtained from a mean-field potential, so the single-particle radial normalization and shape enter the ANC through that matrix element [d64215s0p0]. The node structure of the single-particle orbitals alters the surface and tail behavior of the radial wave function and so changes the contribution of that orbital to the overall ANC or spectroscopic strength [d70976s0p0].

sub_answers.sub_question: In the R‑matrix description of a resonant nuclear state, how are the observed partial and total widths written in terms of channel reduced widths (gamma) and the chosen channel radius a; include the definitions of reduced width amplitude, boundary condition constant, and the formula connecting formal and observed widths?

When using mirror symmetry to infer neutron resonance parameters from proton ANC measurements, how do the Coulomb-modified asymptotic wave functions (including Whittaker or Coulomb functions, Sommerfeld parameter eta, and Coulomb barrier penetration factors) alter the mapping between a measured proton ANC and the equivalent neutron resonance reduced width?
sub_answers.text: Coulomb-modified asymptotic wave functions determine the exterior behavior of charged-particle bound and scattering states through Coulomb functions that appear in analytical expressions for decay and capture, and these Coulomb functions enter the mapping between a measured proton ANC and any equivalent neutral-particle quantity [d41083s0p0]. Long-range Coulomb effects produce a pole at the separation energy and a very extended radial integral that peaks at large radii, so Coulomb barrier penetration and the Sommerfeld-parameter-dependent Coulomb functions modify how the proton ANC samples interior versus exterior structure when relating to a neutron reduced width [d148282s0p0].

sub_answers.sub_question: What experimental procedures and reaction-model inputs (choice of optical potentials, peripheral kinematics, DWBA/ADWA analysis, ANC normalization against single-particle form factors) are used to extract ANCs from peripheral transfer reactions such as (d,p) and (3He,d), and how are uncertainties from non-peripherality and compound contributions quantified?
sub_answers.text: Extracted ANCs for peripheral capture are obtained by using single-particle bound and scattering wave functions from a chosen mean-field or optical potential to compute the reduced transfer matrix element for reactions such as (d,p) or (3He,d) [d64215s0p0]. Fits of scattering or transfer observables to parametrized amplitudes and to phase shifts are used to determine ANCs and their uncertainties, and large error bars in ANC values can arise from the fitting procedure and model assumptions in transfer analyses [d69413s0p0].

sub_answers.sub_question: List and explain the core approximations made when computing ANCs and decay widths using single-channel local potential models (e.g., use of a real Woods–Saxon potential, neglect of channel coupling, fixed channel radius, single-particle spectroscopic factor assumption, and omission of antisymmetrization/coupling to continuum) and discuss how each approximation typically biases the resulting ANC or width.
sub_answers.text: Single-channel local potential models commonly use a single-particle real mean-field potential such as Woods–Saxon to generate bound and scattering radial wave functions [d64215s0p0]. These models neglect explicit channel coupling and continuum mixing that are necessary to represent resonant (Gamow) states and their width contributions in a complete Berggren basis [d2984s0p0]. Fixed-radius approximations and single-particle spectroscopic-factor assumptions ignore dynamical coupling and many-body correlations that modify the asymptotic normalization and therefore can bias ANC or width estimates [d70976s0p0]. Use of an effective local potential form (for example the Frahn or other solvable forms) provides analytic half-life or width formulae but can miss antisymmetrization and compound-channel effects and thereby mis-estimate decay widths when those effects are important [d41083s0p0].
